title: Knowledge Check 1: Lessons 1-8
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 1-8 of the agentic-ai series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: What single property best distinguishes an agent from a workflow?
options: The model, not your code, decides the path
The system includes at least one call to a language model
The system can handle more than one request per session
The system was assembled with a modern agent framework
questions.explanation: An agent is defined by who decides the path: the model directs its own process and tool use at runtime, while in a workflow your code fixes the path and the model only fills the steps.

questions.question: When the steps of a task can all be enumerated up front, why is a workflow usually the better choice than an agent?
options: It removes the need for any model calls at runtime
It guarantees the task can never fail
It is cheaper, faster, and easier to test
It requires no token budget to operate
questions.explanation: For a known path, agentic autonomy trades latency and cost for flexibility you will not use, so the simpler workflow is more reliable and cheaper.

questions.question: In an agent loop, what is the reliable way to confirm the goal has actually been met?
options: Trust the model's own confident assessment that it is done
Count how many iterations the loop has run
Add a deterministic gate that verifies the result
Check that the context window is not yet full
questions.explanation: The model's judgment that it is finished can be confidently wrong, so a deterministic external gate must verify the result before the loop declares success.

questions.question: Why does the same information cost more tokens when written as JSON than as prose?
options: Braces, quotes, and colons each tend to become their own token
The model must translate the JSON into natural language before reading it
JSON requires a larger context window to store
JSON is encrypted before the model reads it
questions.explanation: Tokenizers tend to break structural characters into their own tokens, so the same facts cost roughly twice as much when formatted as JSON.

questions.question: Where should debugging start when an agent gives inconsistent or wrong answers?
options: Lower the temperature so the model samples more deterministically
Increase the maximum output token limit
Check that the needed information is present in the context
Switch to a larger and more capable model tier
questions.explanation: Temperature only reshapes how the model samples among what it already knows; it cannot supply information that is missing from the context or buried where the model will not use it.

questions.question: A response is slow before the first token appears. Which phase is the bottleneck?
options: Decode, where output tokens are generated one at a time
Temperature, which adds randomness to each sampling step
Caching, which reprocesses the static prefix on every call
Prefill, where the whole input is processed first
questions.explanation: Prefill processes the whole input to produce the first token, so a slow start points to a prompt that is too long; slowness while streaming is a decode problem instead.

questions.question: The while loop that repeatedly calls the model and executes tools is best understood as whose responsibility?
options: Runtime or framework code, not something you write
A portion you must hand-code yourself for every agent you build
A detail that varies by which model you choose
The same thing as the system prompt you author
questions.explanation: The loop itself is runtime code; your work lives in what the loop touches, such as tools and schemas, state, stopping criteria, logging, and memory.

questions.question: Which set of concerns is the code you actually own in an agent?
options: The loop's iteration order and model selection
Tool schemas, state, stopping criteria, logging, and memory
The provider's network stack, tokenization layer, and rate limits
The model weights and inference hardware
questions.explanation: The runtime supplies the loop, but the tool schemas, state handling, stopping criteria, telemetry, and memory layer are yours to design and maintain.

questions.question: Why is a hard stopping condition essential in a production agent loop?
options: It keeps the model from changing or overwriting its own instructions
It guarantees every step produces a correct result
It removes the need to validate tool output
It prevents the loop from running indefinitely and burning budget
questions.explanation: A loop with no exit can keep retrying and spending tokens without converging, so a max-iteration or budget limit bounds the run.

questions.question: What is the role of a system prompt in an agent?
options: A one-time instruction sent only on the very first turn
The persistent instruction block used on every turn
A fallback used only when the model fails
An optional courtesy message shown to the user
questions.explanation: Because the loop re-sends it on each turn, the system prompt acts as the agent's constitution: the durable role, rules, and output format it obeys throughout.

questions.question: A model keeps producing worse output as more instructions are added to the prompt. What does this reflect?
options: Each added token depletes a finite attention budget and degrades recall
The model runs out of storage space for new instructions once the prompt grows long
The prompt text is being translated into another language
The system has exceeded its provider rate limit
questions.explanation: Recall falls as the context fills, so redundant context spends attention that the model needs for the actual task.

questions.question: A model cannot emit the required output format no matter how the prompt is reworded. What does this indicate?
options: A knowledge gap that retrieval would fix
A behavior gap that fine-tuning would fix
A reliability gap that a deterministic workflow gate would fix
A capability gap that only a different model fixes
questions.explanation: No wording change can supply a token sequence the model cannot produce, so an inability to emit a format is a capability gap answered by model selection or enforced output.

questions.question: Why does an agent's input bill grow so quickly over a long run?
options: Every iteration resends the accumulated context
The model reprocesses its full weights on every single step
Tool outputs are billed at a flat per-call fee
Caching multiplies the number of input tokens sent
questions.explanation: Each iteration resends the system prompt, history, and prior tool results, so the input side balloons as the loop continues, while the output side stays comparatively small.

questions.question: To make prompt caching effective, how should a prompt be ordered?
options: Variable content first, followed by the static content
Static content first, then the variable content
Newest message first, oldest message last
Longest sections first, shortest sections last
questions.explanation: Caching reuses an identical prefix, so keeping the static system prompt and tool definitions first and the variable user data last preserves cache hits.

questions.question: Why does context engineering tend to beat simply buying a larger context window?
options: Larger windows are billed at a flat rate regardless of use
Models ignore any content placed beyond the system prompt
Cost grows quadratically and recall drops as it fills
Larger windows cannot hold structured data
questions.explanation: Attention cost rises faster than the input, and models underuse information in the middle of long inputs, so curating fewer high-signal tokens beats stuffing the window.

questions.question: What is the difference between a routing destination and a router?
options: A destination runs a request; the router picks which one
A destination decides routing; the router only measures latency
A destination is a local model; a router is a managed service
A destination and a router are two names for the same thing
questions.explanation: A destination is a place a request runs, while the router is the decision layer that chooses among destinations, so calling one provider directly is an integration, not routing.

questions.question: Why is routing by capability tier rather than by model name more durable?
options: Tier names are shorter and easier to type
Tiers hide the cost of every request from the bill
Tiers guarantee that the cheapest available model is always chosen
Tier config can be remapped without touching routing logic
questions.explanation: Names and their relative quality rotate quickly, so separating the stable decision (small, medium, large) from the model it resolves to keeps routing logic valid.

questions.question: What is a fallback chain unable to detect on its own?
options: A provider returning a 5xx error
A request that times out before responding
A rate-limited endpoint enforcing a quota
A successful but confidently wrong answer
questions.explanation: Fallbacks react to transport failures like errors and timeouts; a 200 response carrying a wrong answer looks fine, so catching it needs a separate quality check.

questions.question: What does JSON mode guarantee about a response?
options: That it is valid JSON, not that it matches a schema
That every required field is present and correctly typed
That the model selected the correct tool for the task
That the response contains no markdown formatting
questions.explanation: JSON mode only ensures the output parses, so it can still have wrong keys or missing fields; you must validate against your schema to trust it.

questions.question: In tool calling, which party actually executes the tool?
options: The model, as part of generating the call
Your application code after it validates them
The provider's platform acting on the model's behalf as it generates
The tool schema itself during parsing
questions.explanation: The model only proposes a structured call; your code validates and executes it, which keeps the model safely unable to act on your systems directly.

questions.question: When is function calling the right choice over Structured Outputs?
options: When formatting the final answer that is shown to the user
When the output only needs to be valid JSON
When the model must pick and call one of your tools
When no external data is involved
questions.explanation: Function calling adds tool selection on top of schema enforcement, so use it when the output is an action to execute rather than an answer to display.

questions.question: What does it mean to treat a tool schema as an operational contract?
options: It defines the inputs, outputs, and error path
It locks the tool to a single model provider
It documents the tool only for human developers
It removes the need to validate arguments at runtime
questions.explanation: The schema is the agreement among the model, your application, and the backend, and its error path is part of that agreement rather than an afterthought.

questions.question: Why is the description field so important in a tool schema?
options: It sets the token price charged for the call
It tells the model when to use the tool and when not to
It encrypts the arguments before execution
It determines where the tool appears in the available list
questions.explanation: The description is what the model reasons over when choosing a tool, so covering when not to use it prevents the model from reaching the tool in the wrong situation.

questions.question: A write tool times out after the server already processed the request. What prevents a retry from duplicating the operation?
options: An exponential backoff with full jitter
A retry budget shared across the turn
An idempotency key that returns the first result
A circuit breaker that pauses traffic to the failing provider
questions.explanation: An idempotency key lets a retry return the first result instead of executing the write again, which is why state-mutating tools must be safe to repeat.
